what_it_does: Edge AI chips (small, power-constrained processors in phones, cameras, or IoT devices) run neural network inference by executing each layer of the network in sequence; one way to save energy is to keep the output of one layer in the chip's fast on-chip memory (SRAM — a small, quick scratchpad) so it can be fed directly to the next layer without writing to and reading from the slow, power-hungry off-chip memory (DRAM — the large main memory). The difficulty is knowing how deep to chain layers together: going too deep overflows the small SRAM and forces more off-chip traffic, not less. EDA is a compiler framework (a piece of software that translates a neural network description into chip instructions) that automatically finds the right depth for each segment of the network given the chip's SRAM size. It splits the network graph into subgraphs, models the cost of each candidate depth, and groups compatible operations to keep the math units busy, producing an efficient schedule without manual tuning.
